t: Expeditions map making, for people who have never done it
s: A plain-language guide to building custom maps for Expeditions: A MudRunner Game. Start with a map that loads, then make it good.
x: Make a map for Expeditions # Saber shipped a map editor with the game and a set of official guides to go with it. The guides are accurate. They are also written field by field, in the order the software stores things, which means you can read four pages about deploy zones and still not know what a deploy zone is for. This guide is the other way round. It explains what a thing is and what it is for , then tells you which fields to fill in. It assumes you have never opened the editor. Read this first if you read nothing else # Two rules save more time than everything else on this site combined. Get a map that loads before you make it pretty. A map needs a shape, one deploy zone and one expedition. That is it. Build that on your first day, pack it, and drive around an empty landscape. Now you have a foundation. People who spend three weeks sculpting a canyon and then try to make it load spend the next three weeks finding out why it does not. Your map exists in three places at once , and they drift apart from each other constantly. Almost every “I fixed it and nothing changed” story comes from editing the wrong copy. Read that page early . Where to start # What you need The editor, the folders, and roughly how long things take. Where everything lives Three copies of your map, and which one to edit. Read this one early. Make a map that loads The shortest path from nothing to driving around your own terrain. Something is broken Symptom to cause. Start here when the game misbehaves. Porting a SnowRunner truck The meshes just work. The textures do not, and that is the whole story. Using AI with the editor The scripts and agent skills, what they are good at, and what they must not be trusted with. x: The tools # Everything you need ships with the game. There is nothing to buy and nothing to download. Tool Where What it does Map editor Sources\BinEditor\ExpeditionsEditor.exe terrain, objects, roads, water, and placing the zones Zone settings tool Sources\BinEditor\ZoneSettingsEditor.exe the properties on those zones, plus all objectives. Opens from the editor’s toolbar Resource converter Sources\Bin\ResourceConverter.exe converts and compiles assets Type schema Sources\BinEditor\meta_desc_ssl.ps not a tool, a text file. Every type the editor understands, and the final word when a guide and the game disagree Two of those deserve a note. The zone settings tool is a separate program. When the official guide says a feature does not exist, the schema sometimes disagrees, and the schema is what the software actually runs on. s: Your map exists in three places at once and they drift apart. This is the single most common source of wasted days, so it comes before anything else.
x: Your map is not one thing in one folder. It exists in three places, they hold different data, and they fall out of step with each other constantly. Almost every “I fixed it and nothing changed” story ends here. So does almost every “it worked yesterday”. Learn this page and you will skip a category of problem entirely. The three copies # All three live under Documents\My Games\Expeditions\Media\ . Folder What it is Who writes it Who reads it prebuild\<level>\ The source. Your real work lives here The editor, when you save The editor, when you open the map levels\<Level>\ The staging copy. What the zone settings tool shows you, and what the packer reads The editor and the zone tool The packer Mods\<Level>.pak The product. A zip archive The packer The game Read that last column again. The game only ever reads the .pak . Nothing you do in prebuild or levels changes what you see when you press Deploy until you pack again. The mistake everyone makes once You find a bad value, you fix it in the .pak because that is the file the game reads, and it works. Then you pack the map again and your fix is gone, because the pack was built from the source, which you never touched. Fix the source. Then pack. Editing the pak is for emergencies, not for work you want to keep. The flow, in one direction # you, in the editor │ save ▼ prebuild\<level>\ ← the source. edit here. │ the editor copies forward ▼ levels\<Level>\ ← staging. the zone tool reads this. │ Pack (about 25 minutes) ▼ Mods\<Level>.pak ← the game reads only this. It flows one way. There is no “sync back”. Closing the editor is a write, not a stop # This one costs people a whole evening. While the editor has your map open, it holds the entire map in memory. s: The shortest path from nothing to driving around your own terrain. Do this before you make anything look good.
x: A playable Expeditions map needs exactly two things: one expedition one deploy zone That is the entire requirement. documented Not a mission, not an objective, not a reward. And the expedition is allowed to be a Free Roam one, which is the simplest possible kind. So the smallest map that works is “here is some ground, drive on it” . Build that first. It proves the whole chain works, from editor to pack to deploy, before you invest real time in anything. Why this order matters # Packing takes about 25 minutes. If you sculpt for a week and only then try to load the map, every problem you find costs half an hour to test a fix for, and you will have several problems, and you will not know which of a week’s changes caused any of them. Get to “I can drive on it” on day one. Then every later problem has a short list of suspects: whatever you did since it last worked. The five steps # 1 ### Make the map and give it a shape Create a new map in the editor and raise some terrain. Do not make it good. A lumpy field is fine. You want geometry that exists, not geometry you like, because you are testing the pipeline and you will probably throw this away. 2 ### Place a deploy zone In the map editor, place a zone object where you want trucks to arrive, and give it an **Id**. Pick a name without spaces or punctuation, something like `main_deploy`. Note it exactly, because the next step has to match it character for character. Put it on reasonably flat ground, and sit it slightly **above** the terrain surface rather than exactly on it. documented Zones that intersect the ground cause collision problems for arriving trucks. 3 ### Tell the game that zone is a deploy point Open the zone settings tool. Find your zone by its Id and give it the **`ZonePropertyDeploy`** property. Set: - `default

s: Heightmaps, the tile system, and why editing the file you think is the terrain often changes nothing.
x: The editor does not build terrain from the large master images you might expect. It builds it from tiles , one per chunk of the map, and it reads them when the map is opened rather than when you press Rebuild Terrain. Planned for this page: the tile layout, and why the full-texture folder and the height source are not what the game actually uses the height source is a quarter of the master’s linear resolution height is stored at 16-bit float precision, so the smallest possible step is roughly the elevation divided by 2048. About 10 cm at 200 m up, about 2 cm in a valley why that floor cannot be filtered away, and why flattening a road makes the stepping more visible rather than less the practical consequence: route roads low on the map pushing edited heights back into tiles is a merge , not a copy, because the tiles hold hand sculpting done after the master was written

s: Size, falloff and strength, and why a soft brush where a hard one belongs turns a road into a row of domes.
x: Every terrain brush has three controls, and the middle one does most of the work. Planned for this page: Size, Falloff and Strength on every brush falloff 0 is hard: flat top, vertical sides. This is what builds benches and walls falloff 1 is a soft dome, which makes bumps the classic failure: using a soft brush to lay a road, which produces a line of domes the Geometry Smooth brush, what it actually filters, and the fact that it only cuts when the editor’s hand tools are right, and when a script is genuinely the only option. A bench that holds a constant grade down a hillside has no hand tool

s: Roads are Overlay objects laid on top of the ground, and two of the defaults are backwards for a usable road.
x: This is the biggest single time sink for a new map maker: sculpting roads into the heightmap by hand when the editor has a road tool. Planned for this page: roads are Overlay objects, not terrain modifications overlay nodes are 2D. There is no height on a node the defaults are wrong for a drivable road. Flatten defaults to off, so the road does not level the ground under it, and the offset defaults to on, which deliberately adds ruts how an overlay interacts with the terrain underneath it when you want to sculpt as well as overlay

s: Give water somewhere to go, hide the edges, and keep the result editable whether you build it yourself or with AI.
x: A river is not a blue road. Putting a strip of water across a valley does not make that strip fit the valley. It gives you a water surface. The ground still has to provide the bed and the banks. Get those three things to agree first. Foam can wait. The mistake that looks wrong immediately # If you can see straight, square or saw-toothed edges floating over the ground, you are seeing the edge of the water object instead of a shoreline. The fix is not always more width, and it is not always less height. Measure both. The visible water should meet soil on each side, with the outer mesh edges hidden inside the banks. Check from road height, not only from directly above. Measure in two directions # Along the channel , measure the bed and the fall toward the outlet. A flowing reach needs a connected downhill route. Do not stretch one horizontal sheet down a steep ravine. Equally, do not force a pool to follow every bump in its bed. Across the channel , measure from bank to bank, at right angles to the local flow direction. The water surface is normally level across a section. Follow the bend when choosing that direction; the map’s X axis is not the river’s cross-section. A heightmap is a starting point, not a promise about underwater ground. Its survey and processing may describe a water surface rather than the actual bed. Inspect what your particular dataset contains before designing a lake around it. The road may not be the raw terrain Road flattening can change the surface you drive on. Do not turn it off just to make a puddle show. You may uncover a much deeper hollow than intended. Give each piece a name # You should not have to click seventy objects to find one crossing. Our convention is W00_R000_Name_ReachDescription . W00 identifies a channel; R000 , R001 and R002 ru

s: The three kinds of objective, how they differ, and the single idea that the rest of the mission system is built on.
x: An objective is a job you give the player. There are three kinds, they all live in the same file, and they share nearly every field. The three kinds # Kind The player starts it by Use it for Expedition picking it on the Expedition Selection screen before deploying the headline job. The reason to come to this map Contract accepting it in the world, during an expedition optional side work Task driving to a specific zone that offers it small local jobs, found by exploring An expedition and a contract are the same record with one number changed. contractType is 1 for an expedition and 0 for a contract, and everything else about them is identical. If a job turns out to be too small to headline a map, you demote it by editing one digit. A task is slightly different: it lives in its own list and it needs a task giver zone , a place the player has to reach before the job is offered at all. Without one, the task exists but can never be started. There is no limit on how many of any kind a map can have. Names must be unique across all three A task and a contract with the same name cause undefined behaviour. Not an error message. Undefined behaviour. This is easy to do by accident when you duplicate something, and hard to spot afterwards. The one required objective # A map is only loadable if it has at least one expedition , plus at least one deploy zone. documented And that expedition is allowed to be a Free Roam one, which is the cheapest thing in the whole system: a single stage containing a single field. So the minimum map is “drive around”, and that is what you should build first . Offering Free Roam is also just good practice even on a finished map. Some players want to explore your terrain without a job attached, and it costs you one record. The idea everything else rests on

s: How you order a mission. Stages run in sequence, the assignments inside one stage run in any order, and that is the whole mechanic.
x: This is the one concept the official guides bury, and once you have it the rest of the mission system is just filling in fields. Two rules # An objective is a list of stages . Each stage contains one or more assignments , which the software calls substages . Stages run in order. Stage 0, then stage 1, then stage 2. Assignments inside one stage run in any order , and all must finish before that stage closes. That is it. There is no scripting, no triggers, no conditions, no branching. What that looks like # Say you want the player to reach a ridge, grab a winch anchor, then bridge a wash, then tow a wreck home. You do not want to force an order on the first two, but the bridge must come after both and the tow must come last. Expedition "Escape the Canyon" stage[0] ├─ visitAllZones "Reach the ridge" └─ takeInventory "Grab the winch anchor" ↑ either order, both required stage[1] └─ objectConstruction "Bridge the wash" ↑ locked until stage 0 is fully done stage[2] └─ truckDelivery "Tow the wreck home" ↑ locked until stage 1 is fully done Three stages, four assignments. The ordering you wanted came entirely from choosing which stage each assignment went into. If you had put the bridge in stage 0 as well, the player could have bridged the wash before ever reaching the ridge. If you had split the ridge and the anchor into stages 0 and 1, you would have forced an order you did not want. That decision is mission design. There is nothing else to it. Making a step optional # Any assignment can be marked OptionalToPerform , which lets the player skip it. The usual reason is to avoid stranding someone. Suppose stage 1 asks the player to install a camera trap, which needs a camera trap in their inventory. You add a takeInventory step so they can go and find one. But a player who alrea

s: Every kind of job you can give a player, what each one needs, and the three that exist in the engine but not in the official guides.
x: An assignment is one thing you ask the player to do. A stage holds one or more of them. There are eleven kinds, and the official guides document eight . The eight documented kinds # visitAllZones # Reach one or more places. The simplest assignment and the one you will use most. Each target can optionally be reached by drone instead of by truck, or by drone only . Drone-only needs two settings, not one To require the drone you must turn on both visitWithDroneOnly and mayVisitZoneWithDrone . With only the first, trucks are forbidden and drones were never allowed, so the zone becomes unreachable by any means. documented Also: the default drone cannot fly within 170 m of the map edge, and cannot climb more than 30 m above the truck. A drone-only target outside those limits is impossible. documented takeInventory # Collect specific items from specific places. You name the item type, optionally a specific item id, and how many. Works with custom items. If you have made your own device, its id goes here like any other. objectConstruction # Deliver something to a place. That something can be an inventory item, fuel , repair parts , or any combination. At least one of the three must be set or there is nothing to deliver. The name comes from what it is usually used for: tying the delivery to a model that appears once the goods arrive, which is how bridges get built. That part is optional, and the delivery works fine without it. Two useful extras: additionalUnloadZones lets the goods be delivered to an alternative place. The base game uses this for bridges buildable from either bank. modelPlacementZones blocks the delivery while a truck is parked somewhere it would be clipped by the model appearing. truckDelivery # Drive a truck that is already placed on the map to a destination.

s: Money, trucks, specialists, FOB modules and your own custom content. Plus the reward classes that look fine and never pay.
x: Two places to attach a reward # on the objective , paid when the whole thing is finished on each stage , paid the moment that stage closes Both draw from the same list of reward types. Stage rewards are the more interesting of the two, because they can change the map while the player is still on it. See building a story . What you can give # Reward Gives the player ObjectiveRewardMoney cash documented ObjectiveRewardUnlock a truck or upgrade becomes purchasable documented ObjectiveRewardItem a truck or upgrade, handed over outright documented ObjectiveRewardSticker a truck sticker documented ObjectiveRewardSpecialist a crew member becomes available documented ObjectiveRewardBaseUpgrade a FOB module is unlocked documented ObjectiveRewardOpenZoneProperties a new zone appears , with properties you define documented ObjectiveRewardUpdateZoneProperties an existing zone changes , gaining or losing properties documented ObjectiveRewardOpenZoneDesc the map text and icons for a newly revealed zone schema only ObjectiveRewardExperience experience schema only ObjectiveRewardOverlayState changes an overlay’s state, such as a road surface or a bridge deck schema only ObjectiveRewardZoneInventoryRandModifier alters what a zone randomly spawns schema only ObjectiveRewardsByTime rewards gated on elapsed time schema only The last five are absent from the official guides entirely. ObjectiveRewardOverlayState is the most immediately useful of them, because it means the visible state of a road or bridge can change as a reward. Rewards that never pay Several reward types are technical scaffolding or are marked for removal. They are accepted, they look correct in the file, and they do nothing: ContestResultRewards , ObjectiveRewardAddItemsToZone , ObjectiveRewardsUpgradeGarage , ObjectiveSin

s: How to make the map change as the player progresses, which is what progression actually feels like from inside the game.
x: You have stages, and stages have rewards. Put those two together and you have progression, because a reward can change the map . That is the whole technique, and it is better than it sounds. The obvious approach, and why it is not available # The natural way to build a campaign is to lock mission B until mission A is done. There is a field for exactly that, blockerObjectives , which takes a list of objective names. The official guide says the field is “currently absent”. Here is the more precise situation. The field exists on every objective, and the editor’s own type schema marks it hidden from mod tools rather than absent. schema only It sits in every custom map’s file as an empty list. So writing it in by hand may well work. Worth an experiment, not a foundation Nobody has confirmed that blockerObjectives functions in a custom map. If you test it, you will have learned something genuinely new. Until then, do not build a multi-mission campaign that depends on it. What actually works: rewards that reshape the world # Three reward types change zones, and any stage can carry them: Reward Effect ObjectiveRewardOpenZoneProperties a zone the player could not use becomes usable, with properties you supply ObjectiveRewardUpdateZoneProperties an existing zone gains properties zoneSettingsToRemove an existing zone loses properties So a mission can open up territory, upgrade a place the player already knows, or clear an obstacle, all as the consequence of finishing a step. s: SnowRunner and Expeditions share the mod format, so a SnowRunner vehicle's meshes load untouched. Its textures do not, and that is why ported trucks come out solid black.
x: Porting a SnowRunner truck # Expeditions and SnowRunner are both Saber engine games and they share one mod format. Saber’s own documentation covers truck modding for both titles in a single section, which tells you how close they are. So a SnowRunner vehicle mod can be brought into Expeditions. People already do it — BFW, iX-5 and ULM C10 are community ports. But there is one asymmetry that costs most people their first attempt, and it is worth understanding before you start. The one thing that breaks # Meshes port untouched. Textures do not. A published mod contains compiled geometry and converted textures. The geometry is cross-compatible: drop a SnowRunner truck into Expeditions and it will spawn, drive, steer and articulate its suspension perfectly. Its textures will not load, and the vehicle renders solid black — body, glass, wheels, everything. The log says: Failed to load texture textures/<modid>\trucks/carroceria__d_a.tga The reason is that the mod’s .pct textures were encoded by SnowRunner’s converter, and Expeditions cannot decode them. When a texture fails, the engine falls back to looking for the source .tga , which a packed mod never ships. So every material on the vehicle ends up with no albedo at all. measured The .pct container header is byte-identical between the two games: magic TCIP , version 258, header size 32, same width and height fields. You cannot tell a SnowRunner texture from an Expeditions one by looking at it. The truck going black is the only symptom you get. What is not the cause # This took two days to find, and the reason is that the mod looks correct in every respect that is easy to check. If your truck is black, do not go looking at: pak layout · file naming · letter case · the mod id · modio.json fields · modStateList · signature.cach

s: What the AI augmentation layer is, what it is good at, what it must never be trusted with, and how it relates to doing the work by hand.
x: Using AI with the editor # Everything in this guide can be done by hand. This section is about the other way of working: driving an AI coding agent — Claude Code or Codex — that has been given tools and written instructions for this editor specifically. None of it is magic, and none of it replaces understanding the format. It is closer to having a very fast assistant who has read all 514 pages of Saber’s documentation and will not get bored doing the same operation nine hundred times. What the layer is made of # There are three pieces and they stack: The toolkit is a folder of plain Python scripts. They read and write map files directly. They have nothing to do with AI — you can run them yourself from a terminal, and the guide documents them that way. See the toolkit . The skills are written instructions that teach an agent how and when to use those scripts, plus the hard-won rules about this engine that are not in any official document. See the skills . The agent reads the skill, picks the right tool, runs it, and reads the result. Its value is that it already knows the traps. What it is genuinely good at # Operations the hand tools structurally cannot do. The editor’s Flatten brush levels ground to one horizontal height, so there is no hand tool that cuts a bench holding a steady grade down a hillside. A script can. Scale. Reseating two thousand models, checking every objective in a map, converting a hundred textures, auditing a pak. Work where a human gets it right the first fifty times and then makes one silent mistake. Reading the documentation. Saber’s guides are accurate and enormous. An agent that searches them properly answers “how do I make a road” in seconds, which is the single highest-value thing in this whole section. A full day was lost here once, carving

s: The written instruction sets that teach Claude Code or Codex how to work on this game, what each one covers, and how to install them.
x: The skills # A skill is a folder containing a SKILL.md — a short document with a name, a description of when it applies, and the instructions themselves. The agent reads the description, decides the skill is relevant, and follows it. They matter more than they look. Most of what is in them is not “how to use a tool”, it is the rules that are invisible until you break them : the editor reads tiles and not masters, a CRLF subgroup file is silently ignored, an absolute path makes the texture converter claim a file does not exist. An agent uses them, but there is nothing AI about them — run them yourself from a terminal. They exist for the work the editor structurally cannot do: operations whose target changes continuously along a path, and operations over a whole network at once. Do not reimplement the editor’s brushes. Use the editor for sculpting and placement; use these for the rest.
